overview: The Apyãwa, widely known as Tapirapé, are an Indigenous people of the middle Araguaia region of Brazil. Their history connects forest gardens, fishing places and village ceremonies with struggles to recover land. Apyãwa is their own name; Tapirapé remains common in historical writing and museum catalogues.

periods.title: Violence disperses a village
periods.summary: An attack on Tapi’itawa destroyed houses and dispersed its inhabitants. Epidemics and violence together brought severe population loss during this period.

periods.title: Tapirapé/Karajá land receives recognition
periods.summary: The Tapirapé/Karajá Indigenous Land was formally recognized in 1983. This shared territory was distinct from the later recognition of Urubu Branco.

periods.title: A return to Tapi’itawa
periods.summary: On 20 November 1993, Apyãwa people reoccupied Tapi’itawa, returning to a village site in an area taken over by ranching.

periods.title: Urubu Branco receives recognition
periods.summary: The formal recognition of Urubu Branco followed its demarcation. Recognition was an achievement in the territorial struggle, without resolving every later intrusion.

periods.title: Leaders help shape a museum exhibition
periods.summary: Apyãwa representatives visited the National Museum of the American Indian to choose objects and discuss how their history would be presented in Our Peoples.

periods.title: Community knowledge shapes school lessons
periods.summary: Teachers at Tapi’itãwa and associated village classes developed literacy activities around Apyãwa knowledge, with practical work involving children, parents and grandparents.

periods.title: An Apyãwa researcher studies food and social life
periods.summary: Koria Valdvane Tapirapé completed research on food, spiritual relationships and changes in everyday eating, drawing on fieldwork and community knowledge.

periods.title: An Apyãwa teacher joins the university faculty
periods.summary: UFG records Gilson Ipaxi’awyga Tapirapé’s appointment on 13 February as its first Indigenous professor. His education had included the school at Tapi’tãwa.

items.text: Villages combine access to non-flooding forest suitable for gardens with streams, fishing places and seasonally useful open country. Houses traditionally surround a central takara. Farming, hunting, fishing and collecting require knowledge of different environments, so a village’s livelihood cannot be represented by a single crop or occupation.

Koria Valdvane Tapirapé’s research records Imakopy’s account of collective garden work and distribution of the harvest among families. Cassava, beans, squash, yams and maize appear among the crops he discusses. The account connects agricultural work with education and ceremonial responsibilities, rather than treating cultivation as an isolated economic activity.

The same researcher describes tataopãwa eating groups through Korako’s explanations. Family affiliations, participation in a shared fish meal and remembered group names connect food with belonging. The study distinguishes groups maintained at the time of research from those recalled in ceremonial knowledge; it does not describe every historical arrangement as unchanged.

His 2020 dissertation also examines the increasing place of industrially produced foods. Using field notes, photographs and recordings in Tapi’itãwa, he asks how communities can draw on their territory’s resources while maintaining knowledge and relationships around eating. This is an Apyãwa investigation of contemporary change.

sections.title: Featherwork and the evidence in collections

items.text: The Met’s mask 2017.100 is dated to 1950 to 1965. Its semicircular wooden structure carries feather mosaics in yellow and green, a central blue-green division and shell details around the face. Combining wood, feathers, shells and bindings required several kinds of material knowledge. The catalogue does not identify the individual artist.

The mask entered the Met as a gift in 2017. That acquisition date is different from the museum’s earlier date for the work itself. Its description makes the construction visible: shaped wooden elements frame the face, while individual feathers radiate above it and decorated fibre pendants hang below.

Madrid’s Museo de América holds another example, 1993/02/007, catalogued as made before 1993. It combines a wooden support, stitched feathers, vegetable fibres and shell. Eyes and mouth are cut through the support. The two collections show related forms with different arrangements; their accession records are not archaeological excavation dates.

Objects can also be chosen to explain history by the people who made and used them. At the NMAI consultation, Apyãwa representatives selected palm baskets, body-painting tools, feather headdresses and masks. The selection linked everyday making and ceremonial life with migrations, land and the struggle to return to it.

The museum’s report names Xywaeri José Pio, Ararawytygi Paulo Tapirapé and Xario Domingos Tapirapé among the participants. Discussion of a flour basket concerned its selection and display, not simply its appearance. Their participation supplied knowledge that a materials list alone could not convey.

Teacher Nivaldo Korira’i Tapirapé describes a 2014 project in which pupils learned words while studying practical knowledge. Kaxowari’i and his class drew a fish and worked on names for its parts, including fins and gills. The lesson joined literacy with close knowledge of animals familiar to the community.

Yrywaxã researched a flat canoe with a knowledgeable community member, then worked with children on its construction and use. Other classes studied different arrow types. A gathering brought pupils, parents and grandparents together. These activities made observing, making and speaking parts of the same educational work.

Gilson Ipaxi’awyga Tapirapé entered UFG’s intercultural education course in 2007 and became a university professor in 2023. The university identifies this as its first Indigenous faculty appointment. His path connects education in the community with teaching in a university, while bringing Apyãwa experience into academic work.

A 2024 paper coauthored by Koria Valdvane Tapirapé describes plans for a museum in Tapi’itãwa. The design drew on the form of a large-face mask and a feather diadem. The authors also discuss recording songs, managing collections and protecting territory. Their paper documents a collaborative project in progress, not proof that the building had opened.

ending.text: The Apyãwa continue as communities with their own language, schools, researchers and territorial responsibilities. Severe losses and displacement were followed by recovery and renewed institutions. The map’s 1492 to 1500 coverage does not mark their disappearance, and recognition of Indigenous lands does not mean that every land conflict has ended.
